Unveiled by co-founder Alex Blania at the Money20/20 conference, the expansion aims to protect financial institutions as deepfakes, AI impersonation, and autonomous software agents become increasingly common across high-stakes financial operations. Three Pillars of Verification for Financial Services. The new suite delivers cryptographic identity verification through the existing World ID system. Financial institutions can deploy three distinct levels of proof depending on the security requirements of a transaction:. Proof of Human: Confirms that a transaction is initiated by a real, unique individual, backed by initial biometric verification using World’s Orb hardware. Proof of Presence: Uses live selfie and video checks on a mobile device to confirm that a user is physically present at the exact moment of authentication. Proof of Attributes: Leverages zero-knowledge proofs to let users prove specific qualifications—such as reaching legal age or confirming nationality—without disclosing unnecessary personal details or raw underlying credentials. All three verification layers are built to reinforce critical financial workflows, including high-value fund transfers, account recovery, and new account openings. However, World emphasized that the system does not judge transaction legitimacy on its own, nor does it replace standard regulatory compliance, anti-money laundering (AML), or Know Your Customer (KYC) checks. Addressing Deepfakes and AI Agents. World is also targeting the use of deepfakes to impersonate people during business meetings and authorize fraudulent transactions. The company cited a 2024 incident involving engineering firm Arup, in which an employee transferred about $25. 6 million after joining a video call with participants who were later identified as deepfake impersonations. World has introduced World ID for Zoom, which allows verified participants to display a “Human Badge” during meetings. The feature is intended to help participants verify that others have completed World’s human-verification process. It does not, by itself, establish that a participant is trustworthy or that a transaction is legitimate. Additionally, World introduced World ID for Agents in beta. Built on top of AgentKit, the feature allows human users to delegate cryptographic credentials to autonomous AI agents, enabling those software agents to prove they have explicit human authorization when acting on a user’s behalf. Financial Firms Named as Design Partners. World named five initial design partners for its work in banking and finance: Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital, and VanEck Funds. MIAMI, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BOB AI Holdings Corp. ("BOB"), the AI finance employee for small business, today announced it has raised $5. 5 million in seed funding. The round was led by Mischief (founder of Plaid, Zak Perret), with funding from Peter Thiel and participation from Codie Sanchez, Mark Pincus, Karman Ventures, and a group of additional investors and operators. BOB will use the capital to expand its product, grow its team in Miami, and bring a free AI finance agent to more of the small business owners who keep the American economy running. The seed round brings together investors who share a conviction that small businesses deserve the same caliber finance department g that large companies take for granted. Mischief led the round, and Peter Thiel joined as a backer alongside Codie Sanchez, the investor and operator known for championing Main Street business ownership. The funding follows BOB's private beta launch in September 2026 and will support three priorities: deepening the product's financial capabilities, scaling customer onboarding, and growing BOB's team in Miami. BOB is an AI finance employee that works alongside small business owners to handle the annoying but necessary financial work that usually eats their nights and weekends. Owners talk to BOB the way they would talk to a trusted bookkeeper or CFO, over WhatsApp, text message, Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, or the BOB app. BOB keeps the books, sends invoices, accepts payments, holds funds in a deposit account, and helps owners see where their cash is headed so they can make decisions with confidence. BOB's long-term goal is to be the most useful banking product in the world, and a banking product specifically built for this new world of AI agents, robots, and drones. But they are getting started by building the most useful and safe financial agent for small business owners. And instead of handing owners another dashboard to learn, BOB just does the work for them and communicates in plain language. BOB's wedge has been particularly effective because the company is laser-focused on small business owners who have largely been underserved by the wave of financial technology built over the last five to ten years. Many of those products were designed for the general market or for enterprise finance teams, and they assume the owner has time, training, or staff to run them. BOB starts from the opposite assumption. The owner of a roofing company, a restaurant, or a local services firm should be able to get real financial help without hiring a department to get it. "Small business owners have been an afterthought for most of the financial technology built over the last decade," said Adam Wininger, CEO of BOB. "They are running the business, doing the work, and then staying up late trying to make sense of their books. We built BOB to take that work off their plate entirely. Our goal is simple: to be the most useful banking platform in the world, and this funding lets us put our free CFO agent, BOB, in the hands of many more owners. ". "We invest in infrastructure that becomes indispensable, and a financial layer for autonomous agents is one of the clearest examples we've seen," said Dustin Moring, General Partner at Mischief. "BOB is attacking an immense market at the exact moment AI is moving from advising on transactions to executing them. title: Deutsche Bank Uses AI For Source Of Wealth Reviews
excerpt: . Send to a colleague --> Print (subject to copyright) Request Reprint Rights. This news service is hearing many reports of how A1 is affecting the wealth management industry. The latest case comes from Deutsche Bank's private banking arm. This article continues WealthBriefing’s interview series ahead of its forthcoming AI in Wealth Management research report, produced in partnership with Arta Finance. Deutsche Bank’s private bank is using agentic AI to help assemble source of wealth assessments, with employees retaining responsibility for validation, judgment and final approval. The application illustrates a broader shift described by Yiping Li (main picture), global chief operating officer of the private bank: moving from exploring individual opportunities towards a structured portfolio of AI use cases across the business. “Our focus is no longer on AI as a standalone technology, but on how it can help us redesign client journeys, improve productivity and strengthen the quality and consistency of our processes,” Li told this publication. Turning evidence into a reviewable assessment Within the bank’s KYC lifecycle platform, the Source of Wealth solution extracts, classifies and structures information from different sources. It corroborates and reconciles that material, then prepares a narrative and memo for human assessment, the bank said. The solution is live for selected income-related source of wealth pillars in the Singapore and Hong Kong booking centres. Work is under way to expand its scope and scale deployment throughout European regions. Li said the bank wants to improve the quality and consistency of KYC files while reducing handling times for KYC officers and relationship managers. Controls and human judgment The bank said its approach starts with employee accountability. AI prepares material for review; specialists validate the content, resolve flags and remain responsible for final approval and case closure. “Outputs need to be grounded in identifiable sources and presented in a way that allows the reviewer to understand and challenge the content and conclusion,” Li said. In the Source of Wealth application, references to websites or documents and confidence levels on sources form part of the output. Confidence indicators direct attention towards areas needing closer examination. Other controls include predefined preferred external sources, corroboration across sources and deterministic checks where appropriate. These measures work together to address plausible but incorrect outputs. Scaling The obstacles to wider deployment span data, processes, engineering capacity and culture. Wealth management information often sits across fragmented systems and documents, with regulatory and banking secrecy requirements adding complexity. Employees need training that helps them use tools and challenge their outputs. Li emphasised reusable AI capabilities and governance, rather than a separate technical solution for every application. Future KYC opportunities include document gathering, identification and verification, and understanding complex legal ownership structures. The broader ambition is an operating model that combines technology, employees and controls to improve client service and execution. Li said competitive advantage depends on combining AI’s scale and speed with the expertise clients expect, leaving advisors and specialists to evaluate context, exercise judgment and build relationships while remaining accountable. The forthcoming WealthBriefing report, produced in partnership with Arta Finance, will explore how firms move from AI experimentation to achieving practical value, including the foundations required for scaling adoption.

title: iPipeline Gains Recognition for AI Insurance Technology

WAYNE, PA — iPipeline has been named a finalist for the 2026 ThinkAdvisor Luminaries Awards in the AI Innovation & Impact category, drawing attention to the Wayne-based technology company’s efforts to integrate artificial intelligence into life insurance, annuity and wealth management operations. The recognition follows the introduction of two technologies designed to connect data, automate workflows and support decision-making across financial services businesses: CHARLi, an AI foundation introduced in 2025, and Novera, a digital platform launched in 2026. Together, the products form part of iPipeline’s strategy to expand AI capabilities across its software ecosystem, which serves insurance carriers, distributors and financial institutions. CHARLi provides shared AI capabilities intended to support data analysis, workflow automation and personalized customer interactions. Novera serves as a broader platform for deploying those capabilities across insurance and financial services processes. READ: Kulicke & Soffa Wins Semiconductor Award for Chip Bonding. The integration is intended to reduce operational complexity by connecting information and processes that otherwise require separate systems or manual intervention. “AI creates the most value when it is embedded into the workflows people already rely on and is solving real business challenges,” said Katie Kahl, chief product officer at iPipeline. The company’s approach reflects a broader shift in financial services technology toward incorporating AI directly into existing business processes rather than offering it solely through standalone applications. iPipeline Chief Executive Officer Pat O’Donnell said the company’s investment strategy emphasizes operational efficiency and decision support. READ: The Institutes Revamps Underwriting Training for AI Era. “We are building connected technology and intelligence that can help our customers operate more efficiently, make better decisions and create simpler, intuitive experiences for the people they serve,” O’Donnell said. The ThinkAdvisor Luminaries Awards evaluate financial services companies and executives on leadership, innovation and industry impact. The AI Innovation & Impact category specifically considers the originality, scope and measurable results of AI initiatives. ThinkAdvisor’s editorial staff and an advisory board selected the finalists from a record number of nominations, according to iPipeline. An independent panel of financial services industry judges will determine the winners. READ: Pennie Opens 2027 Enrollment After Health Insurance Costs Double. The awards are scheduled for December 3 in New York City, following a daytime program focused on practical applications of artificial intelligence. The finalist selection recognizes iPipeline’s technology development but does not establish that its AI products have achieved particular financial or operational results. The company’s nomination comes as insurers and financial institutions increasingly seek to use AI to streamline underwriting-related processes, connect information across systems and improve customer interactions. title: AI Is Rewriting Europe's Banking Rules as Smaller Firms Challenge Market Leaders, ECB Study Finds
excerpt: Art & Culture. Technology. Economy & Business. Education. Energy & Extractives. Politics. Law & Governance. Health. Science & Environment. Social & Gender. Sports. Transport. A European Central Bank study finds that AI exposure is linked to 5% lower assessed default risk, while smaller businesses gain a competitive edge over established market leaders. The findings highlight the need for smarter lending policies, workforce reskilling and stronger financial supervision to ensure AI-driven growth benefits businesses without increasing financial risks. Finance. CoE-EDP, VisionRI. Updated: 25-10-2026 15:13 IST | Created: 25-10-2026 15:13 IST. Artificial intelligence is changing how European banks assess business risks, distribute loans and evaluate which companies are likely to succeed. A new study published by the European Central Bank (ECB) in October 2026 suggests that generative AI could improve financing opportunities for businesses while weakening the traditional advantages of established market leaders. The research was conducted by Bruno Buchetti, Christian Eufinger, Luca X. Lin and Ixart Miquel-Flores. Its findings offer important lessons for governments, financial regulators, international development institutions and businesses navigating the economic impact of artificial intelligence. The researchers analysed approximately 6. 8 million firm-bank-quarter observations involving private companies in Germany, France, Italy and Spain between 2021 and 2024. Using banking information from AnaCredit and company financial records from Orbis, they examined how lenders changed their assessments of business creditworthiness following ChatGPT's public release in November 2022. The findings show that expectations about AI can influence financing decisions even before companies demonstrate measurable productivity improvements. AI Is Making Banks More Optimistic, but Not Every Business Benefits Equally. European banks increasingly view artificial intelligence as an opportunity to improve productivity, reduce operating costs and strengthen business performance. The study found that a one-standard-deviation increase in public attention to AI was associated with approximately a 5% reduction in assessed default risk for companies operating in the most AI-exposed industries, relative to other borrowers. Industries such as computer programming, information services, legal and accounting activities, publishing and scientific research showed particularly high exposure to AI. These sectors could benefit from automation, faster information processing and improved decision-making. However, labour-intensive businesses face greater uncertainty. Companies with relatively low labour intensity experienced an approximately 7% reduction in assessed default risk, compared with only 3% among labour-intensive firms. For policymakers, this difference highlights the need for workforce training, digital skills development and financial support for businesses adapting to technological change. Without such measures, AI-driven productivity improvements could be accompanied by workforce disruption and uneven economic benefits. AI Could Give Smaller Businesses a Competitive Edge Over Market Leaders. One of the study's most important findings is that AI may reduce the competitive advantages traditionally enjoyed by large, established companies. In highly AI-exposed markets, a one-standard-deviation increase in AI attention was associated with approximately 8% higher assessed default risk for market leaders relative to the smallest competitors, compared with changes in less-exposed markets. For companies in the top 10% of their markets, the relative increase approached 10%. This does not mean leading companies necessarily became financially weaker. title: Unauthorized AI Agents Are Already Inside Bank Accounts; Here's What JPMorgan, Citi, BofA, Others Are Doing
excerpt: . Major US banks are blocking third-party artificial intelligence agents from accessing customer accounts and making transactions, as reports emerge of software appearing to act beyond users' instructions. In many of the cases described by Axios , customers had given agents their login credentials and permission to access their accounts. The access was not approved by the banks. Axios reported that some agents had also contacted bank call centres, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters separately reported, citing two people familiar with the situation, that major banks were blocking agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions. The claims that some agents appeared to act beyond users' instructions came from Axios. Banks Restrict External AI Access. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from its platforms, according to sources cited by Axios. A spokesperson told the outlet that the bank had not observed instances of ' rogue AI agents accessing our platforms '. JPMorgan Chase has also moved to block outside agents attempting to access accounts using customers' banking credentials. Chief executive Jamie Dimon discussed restrictions on external agents during the bank's third-quarter earnings call on 13 October, citing risks to customers and the bank. A Chase spokesperson said customers should not share their usernames and passwords with anyone. Citigroup does not permit third-party AI agents to log in to customer accounts or transact directly through its digital banking platforms, according to a statement reported by Retail Banker International. Limited, read-only access remains available through approved open banking providers, which use controlled connections to retrieve financial information. The Financial Times also reported that Bank of America was restricting agents' access to customer accounts. Its chief executive, Brian Moynihan, has argued that a human should remain involved when money leaves an account. Read more. eBay Cuts Around 1,000 Jobs After Telling Staff Its Strategy Is Working. US Orders DeepSeek Off Government Systems — Including Third-Party Tools Built on It. Schwab Develops Controlled Connections. Charles Schwab is blocking unauthorised AI agents, including Meta's Muse, an assistant designed to carry out tasks for users. Chief executive Rick Wurster said the firm was blocking attempts by major agents in the 'tens and twenties' each week. Schwab is also developing a more controlled way for outside AI tools to connect to its systems. The proposed connections would let agents retrieve account balances and conduct research without moving customers' money. The approach uses the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, an open standard through which AI applications connect with external tools and data sources. Schwab intends to restrict what those connections can access and prevent them from initiating transactions. The restriction would come from the permissions Schwab applies, rather than from MCP automatically making every connection read-only. Banks Question Responsibility for Unintended Transfers. The restrictions leave banks facing a question that extends beyond whether an agent can log in: who would bear responsibility if it made an unintended transfer ?. Wurster has raised concerns about banks and customers being unable to control an outside agent's actions. A customer might authorise an assistant to review their finances without expecting it to move money or take other steps. Giving an agent access to an account is also different from approving every action it subsequently takes. Responsibility for any resulting loss would depend on the circumstances, applicable law and contractual arrangements. Lenders Prepare for AI-Related Incidents.
